utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, you described seeing Dusko Tadic on 21st August 1992 at Trnopolje camp. You said that he was wearing civilian clothes. Can you remember what those clothes were? Can you describe them to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had jeans, rather faded, and a t-shirt which was not white, which was, as we call it, like white coffee, coffee with milk, and he had a jacket, we called them "McLeod" jackets but he was carrying it in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of jacket was that, a "McLeod" jacket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were very trendy at the time, those jackets, at least in ex Yugoslavia. They were highly appreciated and they were worn by people who were stronger, who were more strong built. They were quite expensive. They were of leather imitation and inside there was a special fur, depending on the colour, the colour of the fur varied. On the outside and on the inside, the colour could vary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A coffee coloured leather jacket with a white woolen lining, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A lining that was on the inside as well as on the collar of the jacket, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have given this description of him and it appears that he is standing or walking in the area so that you can see all of his body, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No question of a part of his body being obscured in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement about this in 1994, October 1994, and describing seeing Dusko Tadic on this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to look at this statement and I tender it as Defence 29, your Honour? (Handed). [To the witness]: This is a copy in your own language of that interview that took place on 26th and 27th October 1994. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A Mr. Robert Reid was present at the time and there was an interpreter on that day, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to page 12 and you see the third paragraph, the largest paragraph on that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just read that paragraph to yourself to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there is nothing in that paragraph there that relates to Dusko Tadic either walking around or standing near the perimeter of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The only description of Dusko Tadic being anywhere is you seeing him in a Mercedes car, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement I made, but since nobody asked me to specify how and what, the question was, "Did you see him?" and I saw him. "How did you see him?" So, naturally I said he was in a Mercedes and that he followed the convoy in a Mercedes. So I was not asked any accurate, any detailed facts, and here I was asked to be very precise, to speak in detail. That is why I do that. Had I been asked to describe it in detail before, I would have done that, but I did not say and I cannot say that I saw Dusko Tadic inside the camp -- not once. I cannot see that I saw Dusko Tadic hit anyone, but here, before this court, I am giving detailed answers and, to my mind, that, the other one was only a global answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at the detail then. In that statement you say in the sentence beginning "Nosio" fifth line from the bottom, if you could read out that sentence, in fact, to the Court on page 12 in that paragraph "Nosio je koznu", fifth line from the bottom of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, do you mean the lines or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Bos will hand it to me? I will make a mark where it is to help you, Mr. Mujkanovic. Do you see where I have underlined some words in the third paragraph? Perhaps you could read those out in your own language so that we can hear what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says: "He was wearing a leather jacket of a coffee colour with white woolen lining, which was also on the collar. I could not see what else he was wearing".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked those details as to what he was wearing, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to see now a video clip. I tender this as D30, your Honour. If the technical support could now play on our video monitors a short passage of a video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hold that there. Thank you. You see on the screen there that jacket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see this film before you gave that statement, Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not see this film by Monika Gras on television? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I am in a country which seldom, very seldom, offers any information. Moreover, I do not know the language and I spent a very long time in the camp so that I really had no opportunity to watch anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were not interested in watching any programmes on these matters in the country where you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was interested naturally, but such programmes are very, very seldom shown, and I watch them also seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, this film was taken in 1994 in winter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This summer in 1992 in the Prijedor region was an exceptionally hot summer, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, but mornings and nights were quite cool.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The description you have given of the jacket, was it this jacket that you see being worn here on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that jacket was slightly different cut. Yes, it is the same material, but not the same cut. It had -- it was up to the waist like a leather jacket. It went down to the waist and that is not that jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems then that the jacket being worn on this occasion that you are describing in Trnopolje appears to be similar in colour and the lining, lining on the collar that you said in your statement in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it is by accident or not, but I claim that this is not that jacket. This is a winter jacket for cold winter days and that jacket is completely different. Whether the colours happen to be the same, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How could you tell the cut of the jacket if it was being carried, Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will repeat it. How could you tell the cut of the jacket and that it was not the same as this one if it was being carried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To begin with, sir, I am not blind and I also know what a jacket, what a short jacket is and what a long jacket is, because had he been carrying a long jacket, it would have been at least 60, 70 centimetres on each side or even more hanging, I mean, if you carry it in your hand dangling, and that jacket was shorter, much shorter, almost half the size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why in 1994 when you were questioned about this matter did you say you could not see anything else he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what he was wearing. I did not say that he had been carrying a pistol. I said he had jeans and what we call an under -- a t-shirt with short sleeves and that in his hands he had and I said nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have described in this courtroom to me only a few minutes ago that he was wearing jeans and a t-shirt, and yet in 1994 you only describe a coffee coloured leather jacket and say you could not see what else he was wearing. So why did you say that in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I stated before this court the following, that I had given a general statement and here I was asked for precise details and I am doing my best to give detailed answers. That is that. Had I been asked what I saw, I came to this court only to say what I had seen and what I had gone through, so do not think that I am blaming anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reason why you only describe those articles of clothing in 1994 is because you had seen this film here on the television, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have not been telling us the truth about this jacket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, your Honours, I did not come here to tell lies because I have no need to lie. I am telling the truth. I took the oath and it would have been a lie (and a very big lie) if I said that I had killed my family, that we ourselves raped our mothers and sisters, that we drove ourselves to camps or banished from our own country. That would be a lie and I have no interest in lying. I did not go to a fashion show, sir. I was in a camp. I was trying to save my life. I was twice condemned to death, sir. I do apologise. You are doing your job and I respect that, but if what you just said and what I am getting in my mother's tongue, that means that I am lying. I did not come here to accuse anyone. Sir, I came here only because this Court invited me to give a statement. I did not come because of Dusko Tadic or for this one or that one. I never meddled in politics or anything else. I am just a common man like all other simple mortals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. D30, which I have tendered, I now offer as an Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to D30?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: D30 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have done to assist the Court is actually have the significant clip printed out so that we will not have to keep the video. I think the Prosecution will understand that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is the Defence then only submitting part of the Exhibit because the video also showed some footage of a person from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have just taken the cut out of the freeze frame that we had.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will admit D30 as the video clip. We can use that as D30A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. D30A will be the photo or a photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any additional questions, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Mujkanovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now we were hearing from Mr. Blazevic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Had you concluded your direct -- I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I had, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You had, I am sorry. Would you ask Mr. Blazevic to come in? MR. MIRSAD BLAZEVIC, recalled

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you are still under oath. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano, will you conduct cross?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you were telling us yesterday something about your relationship with Dusko Tadic before the war. It appears that you did not know him very well, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I knew him well, and the whole of Kozarac knew him well and the vicinity of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You told the Court that you saw him very rarely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You went into the town of Kozarac seldom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: In fact when you gave a statement to the Prosecution in June 1995, do you recall that ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: --- in that statement you told the Prosecutor's Office that the last time you had seen Dusko Tadic before the war was in 1989 or 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the year or the month or the date.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But it was some two to three years before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say that.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did you know Dusko Tadic as a man who wore a beard or as a man who was clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Meaning that he sometimes wore a beard and sometimes did not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You went on to tell us about an occasion on which you saw him in Trnopolje camp in August, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You saw him from around a corner entering the premises of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did he have a beard on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You next saw him when you had been taken out on forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: This forced labour consisted of taking water meters from deserted houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Burnt houses.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Were you chosen at random for this job or were you taken because of your experience as a plumber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They picked me out because I know the area and I had worked in the area.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did the guards who took you on this forced labour have any authority with them for what they were doing? Did they have any documents authorising them to take these water meters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. Nobody ever showed me, but it was my former company which did it.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So were you taken to a particular house and asked to remove the water meter from that house and so on, or did you just pick houses from the street as you went along and went in to get the water meters from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, the inmates, went from door to door and the guards would be standing at the entrance of the house, and we would go into the yard and take out the water meters and loaded them on to a truck.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So what was, in fact, happening was that these houses were being looted, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand how you mean it? "Looted"? Those houses were already burnt, the ones that we took water meters out. There was nothing in the houses or in front of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But, as far as you know, no one had any permission to take these water meters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that my company was the only one authorised throughout, across the territory of the municipality of Prijedor to first build in the water meters. I mean, when somebody would build something, he would pay for this and we, who worked for the company, were authorised to put in those water meters and then the new house would get the water. But these houses, the owner, if the owner would be killed or disappear or whatever, then this water meter would belong to the company that had put it in its place.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: At some stage while you were engaged in labour, you came to the crossroads in Kozarac where Marsala Tita Street joins the Banja Luka/Prijedor road, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The truck stopped at the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The guards who were in charge of you were questioned as to what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Were you in the truck when that was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was eating by the bus, having my breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your guards started to refuse to unload their supplies of water meters as they were requested to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You said in evidence yesterday that at that point you were engaged in taking a water meter from the Zema store, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit after I had breakfasted.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So you first had your breakfast and this conversation started while you were having your breakfast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You were then ordered to go into the store and take the meter out of the store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the store, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: This happened while the conversation was still going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conversation was over by then -- in fact, it still went on. They were still talking something to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But the guard who ordered you to go into the store was not taking heed of the obstruction which was being caused at the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But whether you were paying attention or not, the guard was not taking this seriously in that he was asking you to carry on with your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is, when we came to the intersection itself, we started working right away. We took the water meters out of several houses. Then we went back to the truck. Myself and Aziz Mujkanovic got breakfast from one of the guards, the people who guarded us, and then we started eating our breakfast. In the meantime, some had not arrived yet, but the two of us had arrived. Then they were talking. There was some negotiation. They were talking about something with the civilian police, I think his name was Goran Babic whom I also knew -- he was in the civilian police -- and some other guys who were in the police, those were the reserve police whom I knew because they were my neighbours. They came over to me. I greeted them. They asked me what I was doing, how I was there. I told them that I was in the camp, Trnopolje. They asked me what were our plans, those guys from the reserve police, and I told them that we had a task by the company and the camp Commander to fix the water for Trnopolje and the other places surrounding Trnopolje that had not been destroyed. The guy from the police who knew me well through my brother told me, "Where is the main?" that had been broken, that he himself had broken the main during the attack on Kozarac, and described exactly the location and I said to my team, in order not to search up and down the line which is pretty long, that "I know exactly where the break was, that the man told me". That is -- that was my contact with the civilian police, but I had not spoken to Dusan Tadic at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So there were several other policemen around at the time apart from Goran Babic and the man you described as Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: You went into the store to take out the water meter and you heard a man called Boca telling someone not to argue with this man as he was the Commander of the special forces, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was what Boca said, but from Kozarac, from the main asphalt, the so-called new asphalt, Banja Luka/Prijedor, there was the main Commander of SUP, and two of his bodyguards were arriving. I also knew him but I did not know him as the Commander of the SUP, but as a man who had high education and was working in the local agency for the education. I did not know that this man was the Commander, the chief of the SUP. He approached me and he said, since he knew me, that I was working for the water company, first, he asked me what I was doing and I told him. This man who was with me in the uniform, he said that he had organised with Mirko Sanicanin, my boss, that we should do everything what we were doing, and they should go to Kozarac to mark the objects that have been burnt down for demolition. That was all close to Dusan Tadic and Boca and this Zema, maybe 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So is what you are saying that the Commander of the SUP was arriving on the scene at the time with his two bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The water meter that you were taking from the store, Zema, did you put that into the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember but, as far as I recall, I only brought it up to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: The truck was then unloaded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that, I do not know if they were unloading or they had unloaded. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: By this time how many people altogether would you say were on the scene, including the prisoners on forced labour, the guards with you, the policemen who you met there and the Commander of SUP and whoever was with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were, the workers who were in forced labour, four or five, also there were three or four of our guards that were guarding us. There was Dusan Tadic. There was -- and then Boca was coming, the driver from the company, for the wholesale company. Then there were the policemen. I do not know exactly. There were the active and the reserve ones, those civilian. I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But there was quite a group of people at the scene? You then left the scene with the truck to go back to the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: As you were leaving, you saw a tractor with furniture arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, logs.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: I think yesterday you said logs and furniture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been the other order but they were both there on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Once again the tractor, like you had been, is asked to unload?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: As you are leaving, you hear the words that you described to us yesterday, and I am quoting, "Nothing can leave Kozarac, not a piece of a match. I liberated Kozarac and nobody is going to take anything out of Kozarac, only over my dead body".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Those were the exact words that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the words that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: When were you first asked to remember these words being said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: When did someone first ask you about these events and you recounted that scene to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was first asked that -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was giving the statement for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So that was in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly either the year or the date, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: During all this time you had not spoken directly to the man you have described as Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: During the events you have just described, you did not have any conversation with the man you have described as Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I greeted him or no. Edhem Demirovic did greet him. I saw that well.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did Dusan Tadic have a beard at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Since you left the area, have you seen any programmes on television about Dusko Tadic or about the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on average I have not.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: On average you have not. Does that mean you never have seen any programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw when he was arrested. When he was arrested in Munich, the Croatian television showed that and the German television and, I believe, other European countries as well.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Blazevic, is that it was not until you saw his arrest on television that you thought you might have seen Dusko Tadic on these two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I knew Dusan Tadic well. How should I doubt myself? As soon as I saw him on television I said, "Here is Dusan Tadic" when I was in Trnopolje, and then I told her the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you were asked some questions about the people present there in Kozarac at the scene where the water meters were being collected. You mentioned that the Commander of the SUP was present also on that occasion, is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the Commander of the SUP there during the whole period of time that Dule Tadic was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him going towards Dule Tadic, and when did they get together and what they talked about that, I do not know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Commander of the SUP was there present when Dule Tadic said that the water meters had to be taken off the truck, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Commander of the SUP at any stage intervene in this dispute that was going on about whether or not the meters should be taken off the truck or not that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what you were able to observe, did it appear to you that the Commander of the SUP was Dule Tadic's superior or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you explain that, "superior"? How do you mean "superior"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who do you think, from your observation, was the person there with the most authority? Was it the Commander of the SUP or was it Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you that. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss De Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Nothing arising, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say the Commander of the SUP, that was the local SUP for the village, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Blazevic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir. You are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your next witness is 67 on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, the Prosecution calls Jusuf Arifagic. MR. JUSUF ARIFAGIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you stand, please, and take the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, is your full name Jusuf Arifagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17th August 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac, municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it in the town of Kozarac itself or did you live in one of the surrounding parts of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in one of the parts of Kozarac which is called Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the old part of Kozarac, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the old part of Kozarac, from the history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far, approximately, would that have been from the centre of the town, the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the very centre, from the Marsala Tita Street, about one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you attend your primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary school I completed in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go to do your secondary schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secondary school was in the middle school centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of your education what were you trained as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was, I was a machine technologist at the end of my secondary school training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that commonly known as a mechanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With which company did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Montmontaza in Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They worked, they were building refineries and they were assembling certain industrial facilities and I worked in the anti-corrosive unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Even though you were working in Zagreb, did you from time to time come back to the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all my free time, which means the holidays, I spent in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your family home in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your family home which you would come back to during your free time in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you also with this company work in Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again during your free time, would you then travel back to your home in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in 1980/81?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that in Serbia that you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you by your ethnic group Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 where were you at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you returned on leave, on extended leave, from Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was on an extended leave because I had been building my family home at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was a new home that you were building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until then I lived together with my family in my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the new home that you were building at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately, in the immediate vicinity of my father's house, about 50 to 100 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So for the first months of 1992, starting from January through to May 1992, you were present in Kozarac, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During that time did you see a build-up in the region of Prijedor, a build-up of military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see the JNA become more active in this particular area, particularly around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you also observe a change in the television transmissions that you used to be able to receive when you were living in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during one period of time radio television Banja Luka and through that radio television Belgrade was the only TV programme that we could watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the programmes that you could watch, was there a build-up of anti-Muslim, anti-Croatian television publications and propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In February or March 1992, did you see helicopters operating in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they operating during the day or the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was happening exclusively at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to this time was it common to see helicopters flying in and about the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At about this time, February/March 1992, how often did you hear the helicopters operating around the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite frequently. As I pointed out, it was all happening at night and often they would use Mount Kozara towards a village, Balte, going towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told or given certain information about what these helicopters were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we got certain information. Apparently, they were coming to the village of Balte and bringing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My cousin who was then working in the legal police in Prijedor and Omarska, mostly those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had he told you that he had been involved in ascertaining what was happening with respect to these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that they were invited by citizens, that helicopters were landing there and that, as far as they knew, they were unloading arms there, and so the patrols were being sent there. The Commander of the local police station was sending them and they were told that they were the routine military exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the arms that were being unloaded were distributed during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably they were. After the attack on Kozarac the artillery was active, was operating from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of April and the beginning of May, as a result of the increasing tension in the area, were the people of Kozarac, some of the people in Kozarac, forming themselves into guards, guard units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not really a guard. There were sentries even though there was already Territorial Defence in Kozarac which had been activated. I think that an explanation should be added. The Territorial Defence was guaranteed by constitution of Yugoslavia, and they were attached to the JNA and they wore the JNA uniforms and they were regular units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was a guard unit set up separate and distinct from the Territorial Defence, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that happened later. That was an initiative on the part of citizens that at night somebody should always be awake to follow what was going on in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and that is what I am talking about. Did you become yourself part of this initiative of the citizens of Kozarac to provide guards at various points around the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the time, at first that means, I was only in my village, in Stari Grad, but about seven to 10 days before the attack on Kozarac, a decision was made to create a line around the entire Kozarac so that we could observe movements and I was in the village of Javori.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you wear any sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What arms did you have assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A hunting rifle. Usually, it was the -- those were the weapons who had, that villagers had, so when the shift would change people would keep the same piece of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So this hunting rifle was not yours, it was something that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, there was some reference to "Balte". It would be interesting to know where or what Balte is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will clarify that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you said that you were appointed to carry out guard duty at a place called Balte. Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I was a guard around Kozarac, towards the village of Balte and a separation line, the last Muslim village in the direction of the Serb village Balte. Balte is on the left-hand side of the Prijedor/Banja Luka road about two to 2.5 kilometres off the highway right at the foothills of Mountain Kozara. I think there was a kind of a mine or, rather, a quarry -- no, I think they were getting sand there for construction purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were your duties when you had to go to guard duty, what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everywhere -- [I am sorry] -- just an ordinary, normal guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you given any special instructions about engagement with people or what were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All instructions came down to observe and that if in case of an attempt, that is, if anybody tried to enter that area, to halt him, see who that was. There were explicit orders not to fire, not to shoot, but to report to political and police authorities in Kozarac itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there anyone, in particular, that you had to report to in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was Captain Sead Cirkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was he located, in what part of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that at that time he was in the village of Besici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that you were to ascertain whether or not they were trying to enter the area, was there someone who was prevented from entering the area and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was only control and nothing else. I remember that on the eve of the attack itself people from Balte used to shop in the nearby shop in the village of Javori. I believe they would come there to do their shopping and sit down, have a beer and go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people that came in, were details of them taken down and reported to Captain Cirkin when they came through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was only visual control, that is, when anyone entered with arms or anyone would try to do something, so it was only observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this a formal military or paramilitary type organisation that you were a member of? Did it have a command structure of some sort? You mentioned Captain Cirkin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the attack it was decided that people from the area of Kozarac should be activated, and in case of an attack on Kozarac to try to defend themselves because they were trying to remain loyal to the authorities in Sarajevo, and did not want to express their loyalty to any other state, especially the Serb Republic. Under the old constitution, every Republic was authorised to activate its Territorial Defence in case of an attack against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I think, if I heard you correctly, that you said earlier that it was not part of the Territorial Defence, this guard unit that you were a member of, is that right, or did it change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that the two terms are confused. Territorial Defence military uniforms had already been activated a long time before that in Kozarac, but immediately prior to the attack it was decided that almost all the population in Kozarac be activated to be ready to observe. Of course, they had also been warned against provoking anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka was blocked, was it, just prior to the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a consequence of this road being blocked and just immediately prior to the attack on Kozarac, did the guard unit that you were a member of establish a checkpoint at Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the second group of people, that is, those directly from Kozarusa had certain duties and that they only monitored it, since the road was blocked, only at the place called Orlovci, that any attempt of the inhabitants of Kozarac to go to their municipality was prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a check point established in the direction of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was also observation there, but I was not at that guard point so I do not know whether it was a typical guard point or what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the attack on Kozarac began, where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the village of Javori.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all at our posts, that is, we were observing and monitoring the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the place that you were at itself under attack or was the attack more focused on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that place was not attacked directly. I think the first place of attack on Kozarac was in the area of the village of Duracak towards Garevci from the direction of our point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any communication with Captain Cirkin at your guard post when the attack began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of that communication, are you able to remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a makeshift radio station. I think it was a combination of an ordinary police radio, so that one could establish a direct link with Captain Cirkin or the others who were providing the communication from the place where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think there may be some misunderstanding. What I was asking is, not the means by which you communicated, but what the communication was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I did not communicate directly with no one from Captain Cirkin's staff, but I heard from the radio station which was switched on that a man was on the air and saying that fire was opened on them from the direction of Orlovci, and that they were shelling them with certain kinds of weapons and I also heard the report of Captain Cirkin not to open fire, not to respond with fire and to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it to wait until further order or wait till when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was said directly not to respond with fire, to try to protect people from the attack, that is, to find some shelter to avoid wounding and to wait for further instructions. In case somebody tried physically to break through, to enter, the area of Kozarac, then to report again to the command for further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just prior to this, were you aware of the fact that guards had been placed around the Orthodox church in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not this, I think that the Kozarac police was on guard there and that, allegedly, somebody wanted to blow this church so that it could be later on represented as the Muslims had done it and so that it could be used us a pretext for the attack. According to some information, but that is only what I heard, is that the police was trying to protect the church and that is why they stood guard around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the guards around the church were different units to your unit, is that right, to the guard unit that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those were lawful police from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the attack on Kozarac commenced and you received your orders from Captain Cirkin, what happened then, what was the next thing to happen, so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We remained quiet. Of course, we were on the alert. Some of the citizens and some of the people in the village of Javori were all awake, did not know what to do. At any rate, I realised that some order had to be introduced, that is, that people ought to stay in their houses and to look for some protection because the shelling had already started, that is, the shelling in the area of Kozarac itself had begun, and people were on increased alert. They were only observing and they were all at their posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 26th May 1992, by this stage had you lost contact with Captain Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I lost contact already in the night between the 25th and 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had lost contact with Captain Cirkin, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 26th, I took the car and tried to go into Kozarac to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, allegedly, at the time nobody knew where the Captain was. I came across some of the medical personnel in a motel which was under construction at Rejkovici. There was the medical staff there. I found a woman killed by a sniper and her husband was looking for someone to help him bury her. In that place I saw a seven year old girl which, I believe, had also been hit by a sniper in the forehead. She was lying there. I merely looked at those scenes. The police Commander, nobody knew where he was, so I realised that chaos was reigning in Kozarac, that shops had already -- that all the window shops had been broken, people were frantic, shells were falling, and all I could do was to go back to the village of Javori.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was then a decision made to try to do something at least to save the citizens of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time on the line itself, my cousin joined me. He was a policeman but realised in Javori itself, because it was already being shelled, and that the villagers ought to be protected somehow. So we tried to organise other location to the next village where there were already some 10,000 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was an attempt made to contact the Serbian forces and to negotiate with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that step was made. I and this cousin of mine talked, so people expected from him because he was a policeman. So he took a motorcycle or a moped with a white flag and went from that area of Stari Grad. We could see Serb tanks and the army which had when I entered Kozarac, and he went to talk to Zoran Karlica who at that time was the Commander of the armoured unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe what your cousin, the policeman, did with respect to Zoran Karlica as you were looking through binoculars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I followed him through the binoculars. There was an agreement with us to watch, to observe and to see what would happen to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was following him, and I know that the moment he approached the tank on which Zoran Karlica was sitting, I could already see how the weapons were aimed at him, but I believe that Zoran Karlica had raised his hand or, rather, gave a sign to prevent it. So he came to him and they talked and returned after some 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he returned to you, what did he tell you, that is, your cousin, the policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that he had been given instructions by Zoran Karlica to take his wife and two children, take his car and form a column of civilians and then start moving in the direction of the tanks, so that just towards Kozarac, but that he was to head the column. Allegedly, reportedly, Zoran Karlica told him that as long as the column was moving, that is, as long as there was a certain continuity, that they would stop the shelling and that all those who remained in that circle who did not go out were to be liquidated, according to Zoran Karlica's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then, as a consequence of that, did the women and children in the area surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to send people to inform all the people about this, so that people were informed in time. People were thinking, some were for, some were against, but I think that a column was formed. My cousin came to head it. He started his car and people moved after him. I believe that Serb units in the village of Balte, I believe, had already entered, fire was -- and people were moving normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you join this column or did you do something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I headed for the mountain of Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you still armed at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you headed towards the mountain of Kozara, did you subsequently meet up again with Captain Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met Captain Cirkin on 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did some of the people in your group then make plans about what they were to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One ought to mention an incident there. As we were crossing the road, Kozarac/Mrakovica, people came into an ambush and an enormous number of people were captured and quite a number of them were liquidated at Zeciji Kamen next to the settlement of Benkovac. Other people continued towards the woods and succeeded in meeting with Captain Cirkin. Some people were for continuing the struggle and others were advocating surrender. At any rate, chaos reigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was a decision made in your group to mount a fresh attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some people were for it, to try to re-enter Kozarac, but Captain Cirkin was against it. He said, more or less, that we lacked strength to do that, that nobody could be done now and that we would be best to split into smaller groups and try to make, break through to Croatia, that is, to run for life. That is what it amounted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally, with that group or, rather, two or three men who were with me all the time, we tried to come closer to Kozarac. However, fire was opened on us and some people were liquidated. Then again towards the night we went back to the place where Captain Cirkin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did this go on for? How long were you there in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was 27th when I returned to that place where Captain Cirkin was. We were informed that he had allegedly disappeared, and as we were coming there, I met Becir Medunjanin, the then SDA President in Kozarac. He was with his wife. I believe there was another man with him called Fazlic and they were moving in the direction of Kozarac. I never saw him again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then stay in the forest for some period of days, a number of days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not in that part. I tried to cross again the road, Kozarac/Mrakovica, and go back to my village to see what had happened or, rather, I tried to go there to see what had happened with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the forest that you stayed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a forest which people called Tadica Suma.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you in this forest for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that forest I stayed for about two or three days and then I tried to cross the road Prijedor/Banja Luka, because I had already received some information that my younger brother had been captured and put in the Trnopolje camp. So I tried to cross the road and I managed to do that. I reach the village of Mujkanovici. There, from my aunt, that is, my mother's sister, I learnt that mine had spent sometime in the camp of Trnopolje, that my father, since he was already 65 years of age, had managed to obtain some kind of a certificate, that, at any rate, my wife who was already expectant in the seventh month and my daughters and my mother had gone to the village of Duracak since my mother was from that village originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you successful in meeting up with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did succeed to do that. Once my mother decided to risk it, she knew that I was coming off into that place so she came to that place and that is where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you met your mother, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I met my mother, that is, it was sometime in the morning hours, in the afternoon the Serb Army erupted that village. I think they plastered it with shells, and we had to move from there, to move towards the village of Sivci. But then we learnt that Sivci had been cleansed, that all the men had been put on buses and that during the cleanses many had been killed. So that after one or hour or two we were encircled and captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were captured, what then did they do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to a group of people -- I think there were about 43 men altogether -- to the nearby crossroads. They were already lying on the ground with their hands at the back of their head and then the common procedure followed, beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What date was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was 16th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had been arrested and assembled in one place and after the beatings had happened, what did they do with you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All was ordered to lie in column, two by two, with hands at the back of their head and to head for the village of Sivci and then Gutici, towards the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway. Throughout, naturally, there was a selection of music which we had to sing accompanied by beatings and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The music that you were singing to, was it any particular kind of music?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were only Chetnik nationalistic songs which were prohibited during communism in Yugoslavia for which one went to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that arrested you, do you know whether they were regular JNA soldiers or were they some other unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were Serbs from the local area or were they Serbs that had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that some of them were local Serbs. I think they were from the locality called Gradina, or something like that. I knew some of them but a considerable number of them were strangers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they belonged to any particular group or named group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that on a couple of occasions I heard them call themselves a group from Gradina or Gradina group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these men well disciplined, that gathered you together, these Serb militaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so -- anybody could do as he liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were some of them drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you then? Where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were moving though the village of Sivci, we stopped at Hilmija Nukic's house. There was a post or something. At any rate, there were very many Serb soldiers there and I think they were drinking. At least, that is what it looked like. Many people were ill-treated there, beaten, and we were there for about 15 or 20 minutes. Then we proceeded towards the village of Gutici in the direction of the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you ultimately taken to a point where you were loaded on a bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were driven next by the road and we were ordered to lie down on this earth road with our hands at the back of our head. I was at the front of the column. I think that I was some two or three metres from the asphalt. Then a Serb soldier came to me, hit me on the hand, ordered me to take off my watch. At that time the church, the bells were chiming on the orthodox church of Kozarac and terrible fire could be heard from that direction. There was a factory there. We called it Kartonaza or something. That was the paper and pulp or something factory next to the Prijedor/Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were captured were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in military uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any other weapons on your possession such as bayonets, knives or pistols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were loaded on the buses, where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us towards the camp at Omarska, rather, to the locality of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the bus reach Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the bus reached the Omarska camp and stopped, I think, at the very entrance into the camp of Omarska. That is where it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they do anything with respect to the ventilation and the ventilation of the buses when you were in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they switched the heating on to the maximum all the time as we rode in that bus, and beatings ensued so that we were a heap in the middle of the bus. On the way, they would stop in front of various pubs up to the entrance into Omarska, and we had to sing various songs and that is how we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they close all the windows of the bus when they turned the heaters on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a warm night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you reached Omarska, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were there for about half an hour. Then the driver returned. The buses went on the move again. The rumour spread that there were no room in Omarska and they took us back. Later on, we learned that we were heading back to Prijedor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were brought to the factory of ceramic tiles, Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you when you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our bus passed the check ramp at the entrance into that factory. We were ordered to get off the bus 10 by 10, to lie down on the ground right by the bus, to put our hands at the back of our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you did this, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was in that posture and I could not, I dared not look, I could only feel, so that one of the Serb soldiers was jumping on the backs of people, that is, from one's back to another's back and then there were kicks at the head and then there were rifle butts and God knows what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this day time or night time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was day time. I believe it was around 2 or 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After this occurred, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They searched our pockets, ordered us to move into a room. That is what they called a room. I believe they called it No. 2, and they ordered us all to enter that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you entered that room, were there other prisoners being kept in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many, approximately, were in that room by the time your group moved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were about 200 to 300 people. I did not count and I did not care much about counting at the time or paying attention to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay there in that room 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I stayed, I do not know exactly the time, but it had already gotten dark, and some of the soldiers came in and said that all the people who came in the last group to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you went out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were ordered again to lie down in front of all these cells, to put our hands behind our head and again, naturally, the beatings started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this day time or night time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was night time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any lighting provided when this beating took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only lighting was that very checkpoint in the camp and so there was very little light in front of the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No other light was provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long in total did you stay in the camp at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Keraterm I stayed till the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were kept in Keraterm, apart from the times that you have now spoken of, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, no, because probably I was in such a condition that I did not need any more beatings. There was one case when we were going to lunch and something strange was going on that day. In addition to the regular beating, as people were going, people were being beaten and then I was beaten too. I think that I was able to get back into my dormitory and then I, sort of, fell into a coma.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were people beaten with at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything that they had around -- weapons, iron bars, baseball bats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who guarded the camp at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Keraterm camp was guarded by Serb guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were part of the military, paramilitary or were they part of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were paramilitary units. Part of the people was showing up in police uniforms. However, they were all the time under the orders of people who wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did guards or people come to the camp from time to time and carry out beatings who were not regular guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the guards organised into shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did each shift of guards have a particular shift boss in charge of each shift of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were some of the shift commanders more dangerous than others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, among us, inmates, we were always fearful if Kajin was the shift Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the most dangerous period of time for the prisoners in the camp? Was it during the day or during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was always the night. The period between 10 p.m. and that they were being taken out and then again at around half past 1 or 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people being taken out, who took them out? Were they regular guards or were they people who visited the camp or was it a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to estimate or see. Sometimes we could by the voice we could recognise that they would be the guards. What would happen when they would call a person out and they would have to go out, we would only find out if they were able to come back and survive and then they were able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe people that had been killed in Keraterm camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often did you see people who had been killed in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite often, most of those people never returned. During the day, that means after that night, we often had an opportunity to see dead bodies in the dumping area which was nearby. Then during the day there would be a small truck -- there was a name of the company on the cover -- and it would remove the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the dead bodies put in the same place generally, in the same area, each morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One part of these people, after the coming and the going, they would just die in the dormitory and we would have to wait until the next morning. Sometimes men would be brought out of the cell itself to the grass that was there. They would be there for a while and then they would remove them to this dumping area. That was the case with Suad Bahonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there many bodies that you observed being taken out on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed many bodies, but the night when the people in room 3 were killed was the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see the bodies of the people that were killed in room 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a large number of those bodies were in front of the room No. 3 on a grassy patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not see that directly but, judging by the shooting the night before, they were probably shot. What we were able to hear were screams and appeals of these people. What has been, what has remained current in my mind is a voice of a man who said something, "Oh, my mother and my children, am I going to ever see you again?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where these people in room 3 came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those people were brought from a place called the Brdo near Prijedor, but that is a large number of villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is often know as the Brdo region, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were they brought to the Keraterm camp, these people, from the Brdo region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
