utterances.text: I do not know the exact date. I think it was after 20th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people brought, were they men, women and children or mostly men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to clarify the Brdo region, that encompasses the villages of Hambarine, Rakovcani, those little villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Hambarine, Zecovo, Carakovo Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the next day you observed the bodies, approximately how many bodies did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a large number of bodies. Nobody could count, was able to count them. Then the Serb soldiers, guards came and said, "Is there anybody who is not afraid of the dead here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man from my dormitory reported and there were others from the other dormitories. There were six of them altogether. Then a large truck came which had a trailer with a canvas cover and they loaded them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see the loading of the bodies from where you were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did it take for these bodies to be loaded on this large truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a long time. After that two fire vehicles with some hoses arrived, and they tried to wash down this grass, it was very difficult though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that the people in room 3 were fired upon. Were they fired upon by any particular type of weapon that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I could see the next morning in front of the room No. 3, first there was a grassy patch and then there was a road and across from the road, so the distance was about 30 metres, there was a table and there was a large machine gun model 84, and there was a floodlight there and also a regular chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what you had heard the night before and what you were able to see, did it appear that this particular gun, the model 84, was used for the purposes of the killing of people in room 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was part of the weapons that these people were killed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From observations that you made after this event, did it appear that the doors to room 3 had been opened or closed during the course of this shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that those doors were closed because they had huge holes which was pointing that it was a large calibre ammunition used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether all of the people in room 3 had been killed or had some of them survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people survived, and I am talking now exclusively about the first night in room 3. There was also the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened on the second night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second night the same thing happened, except what we were able to hear, that nobody was supposed to stay alive, that is what they were saying. Somebody had the idea, they said that everybody had to have their, be shot in the head, and I think we counted 43 shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In total did you subsequently discover how many people, approximately, were in room 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in dormitory No. 3 there were altogether 350 to 400 people. The number of killed, according to what we found out from people who were loading up the bodies and what we heard for the second night, in our estimate there were about 250 people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Keraterm camp did you see at any stage high ranking Serb officials visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I once saw Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What position did Simo Drljaca have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inmates who were from Prijedor who knew him much better, what his position was, were saying that he was the Commander of the Police Station in Prijedor, that is the Chief of Police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it sometimes referred to as the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is the SUP only located in Prijedor or are there SUPs in other locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Prijedor municipality SUP was mostly in Prijedor, and then there were police stations in local communes, that means organised on a local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, am I correct when I say that the structure was that you had the SUP in Prijedor city itself, and then underneath the SUP were there various police stations in each of the communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this time, so far as you know, was Drljaca the Chief of the Police, of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time he was the Chief of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from what you have already told us about the Keraterm camp, what were conditions there like in terms of the food you were given, the sanitary conditions and the general treatment of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sanitary conditions were horrible. The toilet that we used was already flooded completely, and the water that we were able to drink was the one that was used for fire protection, the water. The food was coming once, not even once. It was some kind of a soup, some cabbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often were you given a meal while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning it was not regular and then it became once a day starting around 2 o'clock and then going on until ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the guards, particularly at night, the guards that visited at night came, were they often drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did a lot of the beatings that occurred occur when these people were drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said you remained in Keraterm camp up until 1st August 1992, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Beginning of August. Where did you go from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Keraterm part of the men were transferred to Trnopolje and then another part, and I think there were 107 or 117 who were called out put into two buses and taken to Omarska, because they said before the loading that they were going to Omarska and the others were going to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you placed in a bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did the bus go to that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That bus was going from that camp to a place that we called, it is a bus stop, I just forgot now, it was towards Banja Luka and then it went into the field road so-called that went from Prijedor towards Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taken to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the Trnopolje camp, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about 3 or 4 o'clock. I know that it was close to the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Trnopolje camp where were you placed? Where did they put you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put us on a field in front of the so-called cultural centre in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you first arrived were you permitted to join in with the other prisoners at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, between us and the rest of the inmates there was some kind of a barbed wire fence and guards were patrolling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived there were you given some food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was an attempt on the part of other inmates from Trnopolje to give us food. Some managed to do that. Maybe for a moment the guards allowed some, but the explanation was that we were the ones who had been interrogated and we would be freed, and those over on the other side still need to be interrogated and had to go back, we had to go to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The guards that were at the Trnopolje camp, do you know whether they were part of any particular organisation such as the police, the paramilitary or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore military uniforms, whether they were paramilitary or regular military. In any event, they wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these guards armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sorts of arms did they carry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they wear any head wear that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did, some did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was the Trnopolje camp organised from what you could see in terms of the buildings and so forth in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a cultural centre where usually women and children were placed because there were people arriving from Prijedor and then elderly people. There was a larger building which was a school building where the inmates were. A large number of people were outside and they tried from plastic, from canvas canopies from tractors or something to build something and that is where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people that were outside, they were building shelters in the form of tents, makeshift tents, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it was not temporary. That is how people lived. They had no other way, only to live there until the moment the camp was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why were people living outside of the buildings? Why were they not all living inside the buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because inside there was no room, everything was filled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people living in these makeshifts tents that they had, were they families or were they all men or women or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People organised so that it was for easier supplies, for food, for cooking, so that more people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "more people", what I am asking you is were they families in these tents or were they just men, just women or was it a mixture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were men, mostly men from the same family or acquaintances or from the same village. They organised themselves according to that principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there women and children in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any particular part of the camp that they used to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that part of women and children who were coming, they were staying in the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there guard posts or sentry posts around the camp that you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One point was across the road that goes towards Kozarac in front of the school. One was at the intersection of the field road coming from Kozarac going to the railway station. The third point was on that field road towards Prijedor and also the fourth. The fifth point was on a house, on a balcony. You could see they were placed there. The sixth point I could see was looking from the road Kozarac/Trnopolje also on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the guards patrol up and down the perimeters of the camp that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards did patrol along that road from Kozarac to Trnopolje. They often went into the perimeter of the camp walking around there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the guards often come into the camp premises itself that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see the guards taking people out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where these people were being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think that once I saw a group of people brought apparently from Prijedor and then they took them right away. They took them towards the railway station in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately how far from the camp itself was the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the camp itself maybe 300 to 400 metres in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the railway was operational at this stage when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was operational, but only for the needs of the Serb Army or something, but by that railway the convoys were directed towards the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from what you have told us already, what were the conditions in the camp at Trnopolje like that you were able to observe when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us inmates from Keraterm we thought that it was much better. After a few days we realised that that camp may not look as dangerous, but maybe it is as dangerous as Keraterm. If you wanted to eat something or to prepare some food you had to leave the camp, and many people who did that were not coming back to the camp. Then we had opportunities when other prisoners were found, were finding other prisoners whose throats had been cut or who had been killed lying in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time your Honour? I am moving on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes we will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- would you continue with Mr. Arifagic? Mr. Orie, I forgot to say welcome to you the other day, but welcome. MR. JUSUF ARIFAGIC, recalled. Examined by MR. NIEMANN, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, at my request last night did you prepare from your memory a sketch drawing of the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you label the various features on this sketch that you drew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness, please, be shown this sketch and there are three copies for your Honours, and may it be marked for identification No. 309?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we do, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the sketch that you prepared last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is of the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, I am going to ask that this be placed on the overhead projector. Because you have written the various things in your own language, I am going to ask you to point to them and tell us what they mean. You need to point to them with a pointer that is provided there, but when you are pointing to a particular part of the plan, I would ask you to keep the pointer still on that spot otherwise it is hard for us to see it on the television if it moves about. You need to point to it, not on the screen, but on the projector itself, the plan itself, when we get it into focus. To start off with, can you tell us the road that goes off to Kozarac, where have you marked that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the plan].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to speak up, please? We cannot hear him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you are talking, Mr. Arifagic, you will have to speak into the microphone otherwise you cannot be heard for the purposes of interpretation. So, it is a bit awkward but I would ask you to try to speak into the microphone but at the same time tell us what you are pointing to. So, firstly, the road to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the plan] This is the road to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The road to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And here is the road to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The road to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the road to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here at this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is marked on the plan with the letters "ZS", is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To the far left of the plan you have two parallel lines and written in between it the word "kanal", what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a canal which served to regulate the level of water in the fish pond, in the fish farm. We called it "canal".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is the fish farm drawn on your map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, it is by the canal except that between the canal and the fish farm there is an embankment so that the water would not overflow from the fishing pond in the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving back across the bottom of your plan and going towards the right across the bottom, you have written "mesnica inpro", what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, there was once a restaurant and after that, I do not know how long before the war, a Prijedor company called "Inpro" opened this butcher's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told us earlier in your evidence this morning that there were sentry posts or guard posts as such around the camp. Can you indicate where they are located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this marked with the letter "P" and this is the first post at the junction of the roads to Prijedor/Kozarac and Omarska, and next to the railway station another one was on the road to Prijedor. The third one was also on the road to Prijedor. From there, there was a road to the camp that was a dirt road which went through a field to the middle of the camp. The next one was here and it was on the balcony of a house. I believe it was a machine gun nest or something like that. One could not see it very clearly, but it was evidently a sentry post. The next one was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you go a little bit more slowly, please, because it has to be interpreted? We are up to the one, you have just finished the guard post on the house where you think the machine gun nest was. You were moving over to the one on the far right of the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then coming down, is there another one further down towards the bottom right-hand corner of the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is the next one after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next one was here, across the street from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The school shown as "skola" immediately across from the last post that you pointed to, that was one of the buildings in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which buildings were contained in the camp itself where people were accommodated, prisoners were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the school building within the camp, there was the building of the so-called cultural centre which included, in addition to the hall for various cultural events there was, there were the premises or, rather, an office belonging to the Local Commune of Trnopolje. Here, No. 1, marks the lower floor of a room where Mocca or Mocca coffee bar was, and on the upper floor, I do not know what it is there for exactly. Between the Local Commune office and the surgery was a room where prisoners were beaten and tortured. To the right here was the surgery or ambulanta. As you pass through the corridor here at the door into the surgery, here was a room which all I could see was a metal door. What was behind it, I do not know. Here was the corridor behind the surgery, and here was a store and behind it was the storage space.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, keep going. So what is that building there, that part of the building there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind this sales outlet and in this building, where there was the cultural centre, and all these other facilities that I mentioned. In front of this culture centre was a small latrine, an outhouse, which served as a latrine. Then there was also another sales outlet, but it traded in building materials and behind it was again storage space, presumably, keeping stocks of building material. Below it was scales which we often used to see what condition we were in. Below it in the corner itself was the transformer substation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Commander of the camp, where was his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where it was exactly, but the camp Commander, Kuruzovic, could often be seen in front of this building which says "Red Cross". Often times inmates could see that Major Kuruzovic also spent sometime here in front of this building. There was this building and its point was there, but where his post was supposed to be, I do not know -- either of these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are there any other buildings in the area that you used to see guards frequent while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here there was this road here above this building, the Red Cross or Crveni Kriz, and it led into the interior of this area. I could see a building there and I could often see soldiers go there and come back, but I did not know what was there and what was being done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a fence around the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, when I arrived from the Keraterm camp, this fence here had been put up, going from the corner of the cultural centre and ended here above this shop which sold building materials. Another fence, and I believe it was removed shortly, I believe the next day, so that we could mingle with other inmates here in this area here around the school, and they undertook the construction of this fence here. It was made of reinforced structures or, rather, construction grids, the ones that are used to cast concrete, reinforced concrete plates. So, they undertook this construction, but suddenly the orders came to remove it and shortly after that the International Red Cross arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke about people living in makeshift tents with plastic covers and so forth. Where were the people that were living in these makeshift structures located in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These tents were here, predominantly around here, from the culture centre and mostly up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if I say the area of open space that appears behind and between the school and a cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Over to the right and about two-thirds of the way up your plan you have "WC". Were there toilets located there as well, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were those toilets permanent structures or were they makeshift facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were built. There were holes dug out and above those holes there was a simple pallet that was put there, and above it were two concrete blocks or something like that. At any rate, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the people of different sexes divided in the camp or were they all in together in the various buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were men predominantly in the camp, but here in the culture centre in this hall, what women and children were there they were mixed with elderly, with men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With elderly men. What about the school, who were housed in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the school were mostly males, but at a certain point in time, when a group of women arrived from Omarska on the upper floor, that is, on the first floor of the school, there were a couple of women in one of the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In a number of places on your plan you have little squares drawn with "K". Does the "K" represent "house" for "kutcha"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the bottom section towards the right-hand side you have two little squares drawn together there under the word "Kozarac". Was there a pump located there, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right behind this sentry point was a water pump where we usually went to get water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As you drew the plan, is there anything else that you would draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe one could also mention that here was a coffee bar under construction built by a man who worked for the police. His name is Zdenko Olenjuk, but it was not open yet and here where I indicated the Red Cross building, Crveni Kriz, I think it is important to mention that at that time, that is, from early August when I arrived in the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that plan, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 309 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have some difficulty before you leave the thing, the large building with the arches that we have seen in a number of photographs, I take it that that is the one with "don kulture" in the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We were told that was the Red Cross and then the Red Cross moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The witness is talking about its moved position, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand it, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then the other difficulty I have is the ambulanta, the three windows that we were told about, they really are windows in the two rooms called "skladiste" and "trgovina", are they not? They are windows on the left hand wall of those two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I would need to show the witness the photograph first, your Honour. I think that might be best if I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Because I will ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: He did describe those two rooms as "store rooms", I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I take it, Mr. Arifagic, that you have not actually drawn this to scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not draw it to scale. It is quite possible that the confusion arises here. In front was the store and behind it was a rather small room which served as a storeroom, and behind it was the surgery, the ambulanta, which comprised two rooms and then a corridor here in front, and one corridor which led here to this exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will see if I can have the best photograph located so I can take the witness back to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask just a few questions ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- about this particular plan, Exhibit 309, understanding that you will show him the photograph and, perhaps, clarify the placement of some of the buildings in terms of scale. [To the witness]: Was there, sir, ever a fence around the camp where it is indicated "road", put "za Kozarac", was there a fence on that border ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here and here. Around this school there was a fence along the road, but it had existed before, that is, while the times were still normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the fence remain up while you were at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who manned the sentry post that you have indicated with a letter "P"? Were they guards for the camp or were they soldiers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were soldiers. They were camp guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not those guards or soldiers checked persons as they came into that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question. Which road do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The road to Kozarac or the road to Prijedor, you have three sentry posts there. If persons were coming from Kozarac, they would have to pass two sentry posts. Do you know whether or not persons were required to give some sort of identification or otherwise indicate who they were before they were allowed to come through that road past the sentry post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here at this place people were controlled or, rather, women who from the direction of Prijedor tried to visit prisoners, bring them some food, now whether they directly checked their documents or what they did they do, I do not know. Here at this sentry and this one here, this one was of greatest interest to us because that is where we had to report if we wanted to go out in search of food. What happened to people who came from the direction of Kozarac, at that time very few people moved around there, with the exception of the police and army. So I do not know whether any controls were carried out there and what kind of.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what that square represents with the word "bunar" against it, please? Left bottom, near the railway station, just above the first sentry post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- that was a place which we called a "well" ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- where you could draw water, but we used it very seldom because the well was contaminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It has been admitted already without objection. Exhibit 309 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we have known each other since my birth. That means from the time I started going to school and going out, I knew Dusan Tadic since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he at school the same time as you were at school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was older, but the period when I went to school we would meet at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that you had an interest in marshal arts as well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a period of time while Dusko Tadic headed the karate classes, I was doing judo classes at the same school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said you would see him when you were doing your judo and so forth at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him, otherwise I met him often and we often sat together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You knew where his house was in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You visited his coffee bar from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: His coffee bar was called The Nipon, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also knew his wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And members of his family, his brothers, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his brothers, Ljubo and Mladen. I think that there was another one, an older one, whom I never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said a moment ago that you used to go into his cafe bar to drink from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the war, if you can remember, what was the last time you went in there, approximately how long before the commencement of the war in May 1992 were you in his cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in early May, 7 to 15 days before the attack -- I was not paying attention to that -- that I was at his cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in his cafe bar did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there other people in the bar at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall the nature of the conversation you had with him on this last occasion before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I entered the cafe then and I think that Dusko remembers it very well too. I said, and he ordered a drink for me. There were some other people there. I think they were from Omarska and we sat at one table and a neighbour said, "Are we going to have some appetizers?" and then he brought out bacon and he said, "I do not know if you eat this", thinking maybe that I was a Muslim but I said, "No, there is no problem" so we sat down and talked. At one point a man walked by. We called him "Zule", a man who was given to drinking, and Dusko said to us, and I will try to quote him, "Look at him, fuck his mother. I often give him a drink and he often comes into the cafe and he is calling us 'Chetniks'", or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall or remember the layout of how the cafe bar was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a combination of tables and bar stalls inside the cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a place where you could get food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think there was nothing for eating except if he was offering some food. I think it was only for drinks and coffee, expresso as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp at Trnopolje, did you ever see Dule Tadic when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was when the camp Trnopolje was being dissolved, when I was getting out. There was a small space where we used to get out towards the buses that were parked on the road, to the right of me. Next to the fence Dusko Tadic was leaning against the fence with his hands in his pockets in a police uniform. He had a classic police uniform on which had insignia militia of Yugoslavia, and he had a police overcoat on over his left shoulder. That was the side farther away from me. It was either an automatic rifle or a PM and we looked at each other. I remember it very well. I hurried to the bus and people from the Red Cross were waiting for me there. They gave me food that I was to bring with me and I got on to the bus and sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the date this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 31st September or 1st October. I think it was 31st September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you evacuated on that date with a number of other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that were evacuated on that particular date, did they belong to a group that had been given papers by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these people that had come from other camps such as Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a smaller group of people came from the Omarska camp. I think that even a small group from Manjaca came. In any event, they were all people in very poor physical health, and a large number of the evacuees were the people from Trnopolje and some who arrived from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time of day was this that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere in -- sometime in the morning, I think 10.00 or 11 o'clock. I know that the loading went on for two or three hours and only then the column started moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, were evacuated on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number of people, but I know that it is 33 to 35 buses. That was the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far were you away from Dusko Tadic when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe two or three metres. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did your eyes meet? Did Dusko Tadic look at you and did you look at him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he with anybody else at the time or was he on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you, please, look around the courtroom for me and tell me if you see the person that you know and recognise as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please point to the person, describe where he is and what clothes he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Dusko Tadic. He is in a blue suit with a tie. I think that it is not necessary for us to get introductions. We know each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the best video to show is Exhibit 31 -- I am sorry, your Honour, I am just trying to locate it -- I understand that the best photograph we have is on video and it is Exhibit 296, it may possibly be 298 as well. Perhaps could they be set up ready to be shown? Mr. Arifagic, I am going to ask you, please, to look at the video and at any stage that you need to have it stopped, say so, but in particular if you see parts of the video which are represented on your plan and, in particular, those windows that His Honour Judge Stephen was asking about, could you point them out to us as we go through the video as it is played? Could the video be played? Firstly, looking at this building that now appears, what is this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the school building. This is the store and it was a general merchandise type of store. This is the road to the railroad station of Trnopolje. Again the school building. This is a house that is adjacent to the school and the camp itself. The road to Kozarac. You can see the electric substation in this frame which was down from the building supplies store. This is the store, the building material store, and behind it was a storage room or storage space. This is a road from Trnopolje to Prijedor. This is the cultural centre. In the lower part there was that coffee bar, Mocca. I do not know what the upstairs were for. Behind these trees are the premises of the Local Commune, and the ambulanta and then again the general merchandise store. This is again the road to Prijedor and that road, there were those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this the field where the people had the makeshift tents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the toilets that you spoke of over there behind the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in the frame you can see the back of the school with a boiler room and you could not see the toilets from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this the picture theatre we are now looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the cinema theatre and this is a small structure where one of the toilets was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that is sufficient now. Just in order to see those windows, I understand that the better video to look at might be 298. I would ask you to put it on fast forward and play it through because we do not want to have to go through it all again. But, Mr. Arifagic, when we get to the point which shows the windows to the ambulanta, could we stop there? I know you have not seen this video before, so if you miss it and we have to come back, there is no difficulty with that. Would you look at it and if it could be played fast forward? If you can see those windows, ask the video to stop. Could it be played, Exhibit 298, on fast forward? I understand it is fairly short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is still the entrance into the cafe to the right would be the windows of the ambulanta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could it be moved on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where you can see the windows of the ambulanta and the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you roll it back, please? Just go forward a little bit further and stop when you see the next building. Stop there, please. [To the witness]: Which ones are the windows to the ambulanta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the right, the first I was -- the window to the room where I was going in and I think that the next window, I think it was also ambulanta, but I was not going in there. Then on the left-hand side, left to the door, I think it was the room where they tortured people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I have no further questions your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have a few general questions, Mr. Arifagic. First of all, you told us about helicopters being seen in the Kozarac region. How many helicopters did you actually see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw it on three or four occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did they land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those helicopters flew from the direction of Prijedor and Mount Kozara, towards Balte and Banja Luka, but when they were landing, when you could see their lights, it was in the area of the village of Balte.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you ever on duty at a checkpoint near Balte? I will repeat the question, were you ever on duty at a checkpoint at Balte?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not at the checkpoint Balte. As I pointed out, I was in the village of Javori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the conflict started, how many people were on duty at your checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, there were three or four people and those were not real checkpoints. Those were patrols through the village observing, seeing, whether somebody was going to do something harmful in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were these patrols armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those patrols were armed, as I pointed out, with hunting weapons and people who had their own personal pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say hunting weapons. Do hunting weapons have telescopic sight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You know what I am talking about, a sight on the rifle so that you can identify what you are going to shoot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what you are talking about, but nobody had such arms. We had regular hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the attack took place on Kozarac, was there any armed resistance from the people who were under the command of Captain Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I was not there with Captain Cirkin, so what really happened, whether there was any resistance -- according to me, there was none because there were not on the first lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any orders to you from Captain Cirkin that if tanks came close or in the range of a bazooka they should be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, again I emphasise, at the point of Javori there was no attack of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you not join up with Captain Cirkin and Medunjanin who was the SDA leader from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You think of Medunjanin, but he was not a leader of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I did not say SDS -- SDA of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where the mistake is. I know what I heard. I never met with Medunjanin. I only met once with, but the meeting ended up with an agreement not to provoke, not to -- to try to resolve everything with peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were making your plans, you told us, to cross to Croatia, how many people were there as part of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was a question of smaller groups of people. Where we were, there were about 100 people. Whether there were other discussions or addresses later, but where I was there were about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not 750?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that location where I was, I do not know about a wider region in that forest, but with Captain Cirkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you part of a group that attacked Kozarac as part of a resistance from Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we started from Brdjani but all this ended up near Kozarac, so that the real serious attack never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But was there some form of resistance that you were involved in, in those days after the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All my resistance came to trying to survive and trying to protect my own family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but were you involved with others in armed fighting, armed resistance to those people who were attacking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was no armed fighting. It was all about running away, trying to protect the family. It was all very chaotic and people were just going about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing on re-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to the witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Sir, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mesud Arifagic. MR. MESUD ARIFAGIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may be proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mesud Arifagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 21st April 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that where you were raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what part of Kozarac did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stari Grad, a street, Stari Grad street, No. 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is Stari Grad or the old section of Kozarac located just a few hundred metres from the main street, Marsala Tita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a house less than 1,000 metres from the high street in Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what years?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, what were your duties in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served on Tito's guard in the battalion of honour and then I attended a course for sergeants. I returned from the army and was promoted to sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you serve as a member of Tito's honour guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at Bijeli Dvor. That is also Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After your service in the JNA, did you return to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that where you lived until the outbreak of the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my own, self-employed, I had a kiln making lime which was used in the construction of residential buildings. I dealt in wholesale and retail and, additionally, I also farmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1976 did you become a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about how that came about. First of all, before 1976 were there reserve police units in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did reserve police units exist in larger municipalities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1976 was the reserve police system extended to the Local Commune level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were people selected to become members of the reserve police after the extension of this system to the local communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the municipality of Prijedor and it is SUP requests the formation of units in local communes, that is, the reserve police. Then from those local communes where this is -- which are requested send their nominations to Prijedor as to who could that be, that is, they elect themselves, as all the command, the authorities were in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the SUP would ask the Local Commune to select nominees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was needed at the time, that is how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, let me ask you, is the sound coming through too loud? Do you need assistance with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who would make the nominations at the Local Commune level? Would that be the Secretary of the Local Commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nominations came from the Secretary of the Local Commune, the Assembly of the Local Commune, co-operation with police which acted in those local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The nominees or the names of those nominees would be submitted to the SUP and the SUP would make the final determination of who became a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the nominations and the ultimate selections carefully screened? Were people looked at carefully before they became reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, there was rigorous control of the origins of that man and all the rest, from those places where they were looking for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would that include information based on one's general reputation, information within one's police dossier and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the crucial thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After your nomination and selection as a reserve policeman, did you attend some training or schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that and where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was training for which I went to Prijedor on Saturdays and Sundays, sometimes several days. I think it took about six months, and many, many went there for supplementary training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Between 1976 and 1991, did your involvement as a reserve policeman occasion periodic duties as needed? In other words, did you perform services for the police occasionally as a reserve policeman between those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions in '84 during the Olympic games in Sarajevo, many active duty policemen then went to Sarajevo to provide for the security and then we filled up for them, for the active duty policemen in Kozarac. After that, on many occasions and in '91, from September, I worked as an active duty until the day of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, in 1984, for example, you filled in on active duty when most of the active policemen went to assist in Sarajevo, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a proposal which came from the police station in Prijedor, that we should fill up the vacant jobs in Kozarac because their active duty policemen were going to Sarajevo. This was a proposal that came from Prijedor to the Commander in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you did that, were you paid for that period of time as if you were an active duty policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On other occasions between 1976 and 1991, did you help out the regular police by performing duties such as taking crime reports or responding to citizen complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several duties from being on duty at the station, that is, in Kozarac, because there is a difference when one says the station in Prijedor and there is a station in Kozarac. So that I emphasise, I stress, the station in Kozarac. From, therefore, being on duty in the station in Kozarac, patrols, public law and order and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, now that you raise the difference between the station in Kozarac and the station in Prijedor, let me ask you just a couple of additional questions. Who was the Commander of your local police station in Kozarac when you became an active duty policeman in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then it was Osme Didovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there other local police stations in other parts of the municipality like the one in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a Commander of the police who was located in Prijedor who was Osme Didovic's boss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fikret Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he the boss, not only of Osme Didovic, but also of the other local police stations around the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition, in Prijedor were there also commanders of different departments such as traffic or investigation or patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Prijedor station, there were several commanders, several chiefs, and that is one could call them units or sections. For instance, the traffic unit had its chief, the criminal department had its own, and that is how it remained, but there was one Commander for all. There were only superior to this man, that is the centre, the hub was in Prijedor, just as the police Commander from Kozarac, all that is sent to Prijedor. You get your orders from Prijedor and there is nothing that you do on your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, was the Secretariat of Internal Affairs for the SUP the overall headquarters for this entire organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Prijedor, what belonged to the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the head of the SUP at the time you became an active policeman Hasan Tulundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Hasan Tulundzic, Fikret Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know who took over as police Commander after the takeover of Prijedor, who took over the position of Fikret Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fikret Kadiric was replaced by Dule Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the position of head of the SUP taken by Simo Drljaca and Hasan Tulundzic replaced after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Simo Drljaca succeeded Tulundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you indicated to us you were born and raised in Kozarac. Do you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For as long as I have known myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the two of you are about the same age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say we were peers. He is slightly younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About how much younger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, could be two or three years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the two of you know each other as children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not when we were small, very small children, but later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK, as you were growing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know his parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially the father, Ostoja, because many years we were in the Local Commune in Kozarac at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know other members of Dule Tadic's family? Did you know his brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Having known each other in Kozarac during the time you were growing up, when you were both adults would you greet each other and stop and talk when you happened upon each other in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that a common occurrence, to meet Dule Tadic in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In passing, yes. When I went home to Stari Grad I had to take that way by their house. There were occasions, there were cases in a pub being there together and many other encounters and in the police in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have any friends or acquaintances in common?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might say that, that we also had some friends in common. For instance, Vaso Crnogorac, he was my friend once, but he was a much closer friend of Dule Tadic's, or policeman, Emir Karabasic, and so many, many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Vaso Crnogorac, was "Crnogorac" his real last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, his family name -- Vaso did not have a surname. We all knew that Vaso, that is how he was introduced as being born in Montenegro, and that was what he was called in Kozarac and what we all called him, Vaso Crnogorac, Vaso Montenegrin, that is. He worked in the shoe factory called Bosna as a secretary, not as a secretary -- his surname, I would not care to invent it. I would not know the surname, what was his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know anybody by the name of Vaso Radonjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ratkonjic, Vaso, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dule Tadic have any acquaintances or friends at the police station other than Emir Karabasic? Did you sometimes see him at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The real name is Dusko Tadic, but we all called him "Dule", a few -- nobody said "Dusko", that was too much. Everybody called him "Dule", but it could be "Dule" and "Dusko" and "Dusko" is the real name and "Dule" is for short or a pet name, you know, "Dule". Dule had a friend, Emir Karabasic, in Kozarac, a policeman in the police station in Kozarac, a great, and I think that they could not be greater friends than the two of them. Why, for a while Goran Babic and before, if the Court allows me to say so, before Commander Osme Didovic there was Milutin Vujic, the Commander, he was, and Milos Preradovic worked, who was transferred to Prijedor, to the military police, on the eve of the outbreak of the war, and many, many were friends with Dule Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have indicated or you mentioned Dule Tadic's good relationship with Emir Karabasic. Did that relationship continue or end in the period of time immediately before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic and Emir Karabasic, I said -- I repeat -- were great and even greater friends, but one could sense perhaps one year before the war, perhaps less, they had little contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was Dule Tadic associating with primarily in the year or so before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic, before the war, socialised with Goran Babic, Milos Radulovic, that is the teacher from Kozarac who worked in the primary school in Kozarac, Rade Kondic, Dusko Kesic, Goran Borovnica, who on one occasion had some, certain problems in Kozarac and so .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the period of time you were an active policeman, was a report made to the police of an attempt to burn the Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time, the date, it is difficult to say, but there were reports by citizens, and it was entered in the book of records in the police station in Kozarac, the report that Dule Tadic and perhaps somebody else, I do not know that, reported that the church would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, the interpretation we have indicates that Dule Tadic reported that the church would be destroyed. First of all, did the record indicate that someone attempted to destroy the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not like that. I do not know how it came that way, but it was, as I have said, there was a report by citizens, you see, because the book of complaints, there you entered there all the incidents from the morning until the next morning, and it is reported, whether or anonymously, sometimes publicly, whatever, that Dule Tadic wanted to burn or do something else to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time. I am going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Arifagic, I would like to direct your attention now to the time of the takeover by Serbian authorities of the Prijedor opstina. After the takeover, what happened with Muslim policemen who had been working in Serb villages? Your Honour, it appears there is no one in the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have the French interpreters here! We will just proceed in French! That shows you who is important here! OK. Now we may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, just by way of explanation, what happened just now is that we temporarily did not have the capacity to interpret. So, I would like now to direct your attention to the time after the Serbian takeover of power in opstina Prijedor. I would first like to ask you what happened to the Muslim policemen of Kozarac who had been working in Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the takeover by the Serb authorities in Prijedor, all policemen of the Muslim nationality came to Kozarac and continued their work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did the policemen of Serbian nationality who had been working in Kozarac do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The policemen of the Serbian nationality, some of them who were from Prijedor were leaving, going to Prijedor, and continuing to work there, and some, until 22nd May of '92 two policemen who remained in Kozarac and worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the Serbian policemen who remained in Kozarac until shortly before the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac, Babic Goran stayed, Babic Miroslav and the rest, as I said before, left after the takeover of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a Serbian policeman by the name of Vinko Kusota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vinko Kusota and Marinko, that means the policemen who were from Balte, two brothers-in-law of Milenko Zigic, worked until May 1st and after that did not come to Kozarac, to the police station, any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the takeover, were there demands or ultimatums by Serbian authorities in Prijedor to the Kozarac police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the demand or ultimatum by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was to sign a document of loyalty to the Serbs and then to continue to work under their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the Muslim police required under that demand or ultimatum to change their uniforms in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what way was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to put the insignia of the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the police hold a meeting and decide how they would respond to the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was decided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the takeover of power, did you hear broadcasts on the police radio coming from Serb policemen or from Serbs on the other end of a police radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What sorts of things were being said by the Serbs on the police radios in the period of time between the takeover and the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the attack one could hear a lot of provocations, calling out of names. They often called on Osme Didovic. They were destroying rockets that were pointing upwards which referred to the Muslim mosques, since every mosque has a minaret which looks like a rocket pointing upwards, and many, many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So there was constant talk of destroying the minarets of mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than many times, to destroy everything that belongs to balijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there talk on these police radios about the destruction or annihilation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was that said, what kind of language was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a regular language, as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did they refer to Muslims and what did they talk about doing to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were saying, "Balijas need to be destroyed", talked about the mosques and also the Commander Osme, that he should have his throat cut and many such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the period of time between the takeover and the attack on Kozarac, did you continue to perform police duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you patrol various areas, including Rajkovici, Kamicani, Kozarusa and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you observe Serbian troops and equipment being transported to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Benkovac would be up the mountain, as one proceeds toward the mountain on Marsala Tita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see any of these convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only see them but I escorted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw or escorted a convoy of Serbian troops or equipment to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last time was 22nd May, but there were times before, but on May 22nd that was the largest column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many trucks or vehicles were involved in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that column there were over 20 vehicles that I personally escorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there artillery or cannon ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- as part of that convoy. OK. What kind did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind those trucks they had large calibre guns, those were 150 millimetre -- that is how they were called from the former JNA -- and many others smaller, but those were the biggest ones, 150 millimetres for those who know. The calibre, they can also know what size cannons they were. That, more or less, every truck had one of those, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the trucks have registration or licence indicating who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did they indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were trucks of the Yugoslav People's Army, and on them it was written "Wolves from Vukovar. God is Serb.
